## Introduction

Reducing poverty is a central goal of international development, yet progress remains uneven across countries and population groups. Average incomes can rise while the poorest households gain little, and countries with similar average incomes can experience very different poverty outcomes. This report uses World Bank poverty and inequality indicators [@worldbank2026], accessed through the WDI package [@arelbundock2026], to investigate what is associated with poverty reduction across countries and who is still being left behind.

The theme builds on a long-standing question in development economics: whether economic growth benefits the poor and whether it does so proportionately [@dollar2002]. Extreme poverty is examined using the international threshold of $3.00 per day, expressed in 2021 purchasing power parity. The report examines historical trends and uses the most recent available survey observations for relevant country-level comparisons, while considering differences in indicator coverage and data availability.

The report comprises four analytical sections. The first describes levels and trends in extreme poverty and compares international and national poverty lines. The second examines whether income growth for the bottom 40% keeps pace with overall population growth in income and whether higher-income countries have higher bottom-40% incomes. The third investigates inequality and its relationship with poverty and income distribution. The fourth explores the relationship between poverty and wellbeing through life expectancy and GDP per capita.

Together, these analyses provide a multidimensional perspective on poverty beyond economic growth alone. The conclusion synthesises the findings and discusses methodological limitations, including missing observations, differences in survey years and the comparability of poverty measures across countries.

## Analysis sections

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,fig.align = "center")

# Loading libraries
pacman::p_load(readr,dplyr,ggplot2,tidyverse,knitr,kableExtra,scales,WDI)
```


### Section 1: Levels and Trends

#### 1.1 Research Questions

1. How has extreme poverty changed over time, and which regions have progressed fastest?

2. How do the international poverty line of $3.00 per day and national poverty lines differ for the same countries?

#### 1.2 Data Preparation

```{r section1-data-preparation, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Load the saved World Bank dataset
wdi_section1 <- readRDS("data/wdi_section1.rds")

# Prepare country-level data
section1_clean <- wdi_section1 %>%
  filter(region != "Aggregates",
         !is.na(region)) %>%
  arrange(country, year)

# Prepare regional poverty data
section1_regional <- wdi_section1 %>%
  filter(
    iso3c %in% c("EAS", "ECS", "MEA",
                 "NAC", "SAS", "WLD"),
    !is.na(poverty),
    year >= 2002,
    year <= 2024
  ) %>%
  arrange(country, year)

# Prepare national and international poverty comparison
section1_comparison <- section1_clean %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(poverty),
    !is.na(national_poverty)
  ) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    difference = national_poverty - poverty,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(absolute_difference)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

#### 1.3 Regional Extreme Poverty Trends

```{r s1-regional-trends, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Figure 1. Extreme poverty trends by region, 2002–2024."}

ggplot(section1_regional,
       aes(x = year, y = poverty,
           colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Extreme poverty trends by region",
    subtitle = "International poverty line of $3 per day",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Poverty headcount ratio (%)",
    colour = "Region",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.title = element_blank()
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))

```

Figure 1 illustrates regional extreme poverty trends between 2002 and 2024, measured using the international poverty threshold of $3.00 per day at 2021 purchasing power parity. Global poverty declined from 33.7% to 10.1%, demonstrating substantial but uneven progress.

```{r s1-regional-table, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

section1_table1 <- section1_regional %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2002, 2024)) %>%
  select(country, year, poverty) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = poverty,
    names_prefix = "poverty_"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    reduction = poverty_2002 - poverty_2024,
    annual_reduction = reduction / 22
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(reduction))

knitr::kable(
  section1_table1,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Region",
    "Poverty in 2002 (%)",
    "Poverty in 2024 (%)",
    "Reduction (pp)",
    "Annual reduction (pp)"
  ),
  caption = "Table 1. Changes in extreme poverty between 2002 and 2024."
)

```

Table 1 shows that South Asia achieved the largest reduction among the regions examined, decreasing from 46.0% to 2.6%, followed by East Asia and Pacific, with a reduction of 38 percentage points. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan recorded slower progress, while North America maintained relatively low poverty rates throughout the period.

#### 1.4 International versus National Poverty

```{r s1-poverty-comparison, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Figure 2. Comparison of international and national poverty rates."}

section1_comparison %>%
  select(country, poverty, national_poverty,
         absolute_difference) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(poverty, national_poverty),
    names_to = "poverty_measure",
    values_to = "rate"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_measure = recode(
      poverty_measure,
      poverty = "International ($3/day)",
      national_poverty = "National poverty line"
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = reorder(country, absolute_difference),
      y = rate,
      fill = poverty_measure
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "International versus national poverty rates",
    subtitle = "Ten countries with the largest absolute differences",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Poverty headcount ratio (%)",
    fill = "Poverty measure",
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

Figure 2 compares international and national poverty rates for the ten countries with the largest absolute differences, using the latest year with both measures available. National poverty rates exceeded international rates in nine selected countries.

```{r s1-comparison-table, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

section1_table2 <- section1_comparison %>%
  select(
    country,
    year,
    poverty,
    national_poverty,
    difference
  )

knitr::kable(
  section1_table2,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Country",
    "Year",
    "International poverty (%)",
    "National poverty (%)",
    "Difference (pp)"
  ),
  caption = "Table 2. Countries with the largest differences between national and international poverty rates."
)

```

Table 2 identifies Belize as having the largest difference, at 51 percentage points, followed by Honduras and Guatemala. Uganda represents an exception, with international poverty exceeding national poverty by 38.3 percentage points. These discrepancies highlight the importance of poverty definitions and country-specific thresholds.

#### 1.5 Key Findings and Limitations

Declining extreme poverty does not necessarily indicate the elimination of poverty according to national standards. Missing observations, incomplete regional coverage, differing survey years and the selection of countries with the largest discrepancies limit generalisability. Both poverty measures therefore provide complementary perspectives for identifying populations left behind.

Data: World Development Indicators [@worldbank2026], accessed through the WDI package [@arelbundock2026].

```{r s1-data-source, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE}

# Recreate the Section 1 dataset using World Bank data.
# The saved RDS file is used when knitting the report.

library(WDI)
library(dplyr)

options(timeout = 300)

section1_indicators <- c(
  poverty = "SI.POV.DDAY",
  national_poverty = "SI.POV.NAHC",
  poverty_gap = "SI.POV.GAPS",
  gdp_pc = "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD",
  population = "SP.POP.TOTL"
)

wdi_section1 <- WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = section1_indicators,
  start = 2000,
  end = 2025,
  extra = TRUE
)

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(wdi_section1, "data/wdi_section1.rds")

```

### Section 2: Growth and the Poor - by Annika Shah 

#### 2.1 Research Questions
1. Is income growth for the bottom 40% keeping pace with growth for the total population?
2. Do higher-income countries have higher bottom-40% incomes?

#### 2.2 Data Preparation

```{r s2_data, echo=FALSE}
raw <- readRDS("data/wdi_section2.rds") %>%
  mutate(region = recode(region,
    "Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan" = "MENA, Afghanistan & Pakistan"))

growth <- raw %>%
  filter(!is.na(g_b40), !is.na(g_all)) %>%
  group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year, n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(gap = g_b40 - g_all)

level <- raw %>%
  filter(!is.na(b40), !is.na(gdp_pc), b40 > 0, gdp_pc > 0) %>%
  group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year, n = 1) %>% ungroup()

n_g       <- nrow(growth)
pct_above <- round(mean(growth$gap > 0) * 100)
med_gap   <- round(median(growth$gap), 1)
mean_b40  <- round(mean(growth$g_b40), 2)
mean_all  <- round(mean(growth$g_all), 2)
n_l       <- nrow(level)
r_l       <- round(cor(log(level$gdp_pc), log(level$b40)), 2)
```

#### 2.3 Bottom-40% Income Growth

Figure 3 compares annualised income growth for the bottom 40% with growth for the total population across `r n_g` countries (latest comparable survey period). In `r pct_above`% of countries the bottom 40% grew faster, and the median gap was `r med_gap` percentage points. Average (unweighted) growth was `r mean_b40`% per year for the bottom 40% against `r mean_all`% for everyone, so the poorest are keeping pace and slightly more. Most points lie near the dashed line, consistent with evidence that growth is generally good for the poor [@dollar2002]. 

```{r s2_fig3, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Annualised growth of the bottom 40% versus the total population (latest survey period per country). Points above the dashed line mean the bottom 40% grew faster.", fig.height=4}
ggplot(growth, aes(g_all, g_b40)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Growth, total population (% per year)",
       y = "Growth, bottom 40% (% per year)", colour = "Region") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
```

```{r s2_tab3, echo=FALSE}
growth %>%
  group_by(Region = region) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            `Bottom 40%` = round(mean(g_b40), 2),
            Total = round(mean(g_all), 2),
            Gap = round(mean(gap), 2),
            `% bottom 40% faster` = round(mean(gap > 0) * 100)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Mean annualised growth (%) by region")
```

Table 3 shows the gap is largest in East Asia & Pacific (1.40 points) and negative only in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan (-0.45 points; faster bottom-40% growth in just 22% of countries). Sub-Saharan Africa's gap (1.05 points) accompanies low overall growth (0.47%), so relative gains were not large absolute progress.

#### 2.4 Bottom-40% Income and GDP per Capita

Figure 4 plots bottom-40% income against GDP per capita for `r n_l` countries on log scales. The relationship is very strong (correlation `r r_l` on logged values): countries with higher national income also have higher incomes for their poorest 40% [@milanovic2016]. 

```{r s2_fig4, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Bottom-40% income versus GDP per capita (log scales, latest observation per country).", fig.height=4}
ggplot(level, aes(gdp_pc, b40)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = region), alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (current US$)",
       y = "Bottom-40% income (2021 PPP $/day)", colour = "Region") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3))

```

```{r s2_tab4, echo=FALSE}
level %>%
  filter(!is.na(income), income != "Not classified") %>%
  mutate(income = factor(income, levels = c("Low income", "Lower middle income",
                                            "Upper middle income", "High income"))) %>%
  group_by(`Income group` = income) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            `Median GDP per capita (USD)` = format(round(median(gdp_pc)), big.mark = ","),
            `Median bottom-40% income (USD per day)` = round(median(b40), 1)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Median GDP per capita and bottom-40% income by income group")
```

Table 4 shows the same pattern by income group, with median bottom-40% income rising from \$2.0 per day in low-income countries to \$27.1 in high-income countries. 

#### 2.5 Key Findings and Limitations

This is an association rather than evidence that growth alone improves the poor, and the measures are not independent, since the bottom 40% form part of the national total. 

Data: World Development Indicators [@worldbank2026], downloaded with the WDI package [@arelbundock2026].

```{r s2_data_source, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# How data/wdi_section2.rds was created (run once; not run when knitting).
# Source: World Bank World Development Indicators via the WDI package,
# downloaded 15 November 2026. The saved file is committed to the repo so
# the report knits without an internet connection.
library(WDI)
library(dplyr)

options(timeout = 300)  # the World Bank API can be slow

ind <- c(g_b40  = "SI.SPR.PC40.ZG",   # growth, bottom 40%
         g_all  = "SI.SPR.PCAP.ZG",   # growth, total population
         gdp_pc = "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD")   # GDP per capita (current US$)

raw <- WDI(country = "all", indicator = ind,
           start = 2000, end = 2024, extra = TRUE) %>%
  filter(region != "Aggregates")      # drop regional/income aggregates

# Bottom-40% income was downloaded separately because the combined
# request timed out, then joined by country code and year.
b40_df <- WDI(country = "all", indicator = c(b40 = "SI.SPR.PC40"),
              start = 2000, end = 2024)

raw <- raw %>%
  left_join(b40_df %>% select(iso3c, year, b40), by = c("iso3c", "year"))

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(raw, "data/wdi_section2.rds")

```



### Section 3: Inequality - by James Costabile

#### 3.1 Research questions

This section is about inequality and and explores the following questions:

1. Is higher inequality associated with higher poverty?
2. How does the income share of the richest 10% compare with the poorest 20% across regions?

#### 3.2 Relationship between inequality and poverty

A common measure of income inequality is the Gini index. A Gini index of 1 represents maximum inequality, while an index of 0 represents perfect equality across a population. [@owid-what-is-the-gini-coefficient] 

Figure 1 charts the Gini index (income inequality) against the proportion of the population who live in poverty (defined here as living on less than $4.20 per day). 

The scatterplot reveals a strong positive correlation: on average, higher inequality is associated with higher poverty. This finding is in line with previous research [@Karagiannaki2017].

```{r s3_fig1 Relationship between inequality and poverty}

Section3_data<-read.csv("Data/Section3_data.csv")
view(Section3_data)


Poverty_inequality <- Section3_data |>
  filter(year >= 2015 & year <= 2024)|>
  group_by(country)|>
  summarise(
    average_gini = mean(Gini_index,na.rm = TRUE),
    average_poverty = mean(Percent_pop_4.2,na.rm = TRUE)
    )|>
  filter(average_gini!="NaN")
  
view(Poverty_inequality)


  ggplot(Poverty_inequality,
    aes(
      x = average_poverty,
      y = average_gini
    ) 
  )+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  labs(title = "S3-Figure 1: Relationship between inequality and poverty",
       x = "Poverty rate (averaged)",
       y = "Gini index (averaged)"
  )

```

Table 1 highlights the top ten countries with the lowest Gini index, and their corresponding poverty rates.

In line with the relationship highlighted in the preceding chart, for most of these countries the poverty rate is very low. There are, however, three outliers: India, Kiribati, and Syrian Arab Republic.

India having the lowest Gini index is surprising, given that research has shown a high concentration of wealth in India's top 1% (@10.1093/wber/lhag013). A technical note published by the World Bank (@WorldBank2025) highlights that for India, the Gini Index is based on consumption, rather than income, which results in a lower Gini index.

United Arab Emirates has a low Gini index, and a poverty rate of 0%. While this may, on the surface, indicate low poverty and inequality, the financial exploitation and tough living conditions for migrant workers in this country has been widely reported (@Garret2023). 

Table 1 therefore highlights the importance of considering supplementary information and data limitations when analyzing particular nations; broad indicators alone may not provide a complete picture.

```{r s3_tab1 Countries with the lowest Gini index}

Poverty_inequality_sort <- Poverty_inequality |>
  arrange(average_gini)

knitr::kable(
head(Poverty_inequality_sort,10),
col.names = c(
    "Country",
    "Average Gini coefficient",
    "Average poverty rate (%)"
  ),
caption = "Table 1: Countries with the lowest Gini Index",
digits=2
)

```

#### 3.2 Income distribution across regions

Figure 3.2 shows the income distribution for Australia against selected countries. In Australia, the top 10% of the population have 26% of the income. This is slightly below the median of 27.34%. The bottom 20% of the population only have 7.3% of the income.

Australia's distribution is broadly similar to other developed countries (United States, United Kingdom) and developing Asian countries (Chine, Indonesia).

The two outliers are the African countries (South Africa and Namibia), which have much higher rates.

```{r s3_fig2 Income distribution of selected countries, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, out.width="100%"}

Income_dist <- Section3_data |>
  filter(year >= 2015 & year <= 2024)|>
  group_by(country)|>
  summarise(
    Ave_income_share_lowest_20 = mean(Income_share_lowest_20,na.rm = TRUE),
    Ave_income_share_highest_10 = mean(Income_share_highest_10,na.rm = TRUE),
    average_gini = mean(Gini_index,na.rm = TRUE),
    average_poverty = mean(Percent_pop_4.2,na.rm = TRUE)
    )|>
  filter(Ave_income_share_lowest_20!="NaN")|>
  mutate(Ave_income_share_20to90 = 100-Ave_income_share_lowest_20-Ave_income_share_highest_10)
  
  

Income_dist2 <-Income_dist |>
  select(country,Ave_income_share_lowest_20,Ave_income_share_20to90,Ave_income_share_highest_10)|>
  filter(country %in% c("Australia","Japan","China","Indonesia","United States","India","South Africa","United Kingdom","Namibia","Italy","Germany"))|>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Ave_income_share_lowest_20,Ave_income_share_20to90,Ave_income_share_highest_10),
               names_to = "Income_share_bracket",
               values_to = "Share_of_income") |>
  mutate(
    Income_share_bracket=recode(
      Income_share_bracket,
      Ave_income_share_lowest_20 = "Bottom 20%",
      Ave_income_share_20to90 = "Middle 70%", 
      Ave_income_share_highest_10 = "Top 10%")
    ) |>
  mutate(Income_share_bracket = factor(
    Income_share_bracket, 
    levels=c("Top 10%", "Middle 70%", "Bottom 20%")
    ))
view(Income_dist2)

ggplot(Income_dist2, aes(x = country, y = Share_of_income, fill = Income_share_bracket)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
  labs(title = "Figure 3.2: Income distribution of selected countries",
        x = "Country",
        y = "Share of income (%)",
        fill = "Income group")+
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(Share_of_income,1)),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)
  )

```

Table 2 shows the top 10 countries with the highest and lowest shares of income for the top 10% of the population.

The countries with highest share all have a high Gini index (far higher than the median of 35.42), and most have extremely high rates of poverty.

Conversely, the countries with the lowest share are mostly from Central or Eastern Europe, have low Gini indexes, and low rates of poverty, barring three exceptions.

```{r s3_tab2 Countries with the highest share of income received by the top 10%}

Income_dist_median <-Income_dist |>
  summarise(Ave_income_share_highest_10 = median(Ave_income_share_highest_10),
            average_gini = median(average_gini),
            average_poverty = median(average_poverty)) |>
  mutate(country = "Median (based on 151 countries)")|>
  select(country,everything())


Income_dist_highest_share <- Income_dist |>
  arrange(desc(Ave_income_share_highest_10))|>
  select(country,Ave_income_share_highest_10,average_gini,average_poverty)|>
  head(10)

Income_dist_lowest_share <- Income_dist |>
  arrange(Ave_income_share_highest_10)|>
  select(country,Ave_income_share_highest_10,average_gini,average_poverty)|>
  head(10)|>
  arrange(desc(Ave_income_share_highest_10))

knitr::kable(
  bind_rows(Income_dist_highest_share, Income_dist_median, Income_dist_lowest_share),
  format = "html",
  col.names = c(
    "Country",
    "Top 10% income<br>share (%)",
    "Average Gini<br>coefficient",
    "Average poverty<br>rate (%)"
  ),
  caption = "Table 2: Countries with the highest share of income in the top 10% of the population",
  escape = FALSE,
  digits = 2
  
) |>
  kableExtra::row_spec(11, bold = TRUE, italic = TRUE)|>
  kable_styling(full_width = TRUE)

```








### Section 4: Poverty and wellbeing - by Yuyao Chen

This section examines the relationship between poverty, life expectancy and GDP per capita across countries by using World Bank data from 2015 to 2023.

#### 4.1 Research question

- 1. Do countries with higher extreme poverty rates have lower life expectancy?
- 2. Does the relationship between poverty and life expectancy remain after accounting for GDP per capita?

```{r data-preparation}

# Set up the data set, end with 2023 as only 26 countries data in 2024 and too many missing values in 2025
sec4_data <- WDI(country = "all",indicator = c(poverty = "SI.POV.DDAY",life_expectancy = "SP.DYN.LE00.IN",gdp_per_capita = "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD"),
  start = 2015,end = 2023,extra = TRUE)

# Remove regional aggregates and NA values
sec4_use <- sec4_data|>
  filter(!is.na(region),region != "Aggregates",!is.na(poverty),
    !is.na(life_expectancy),!is.na(gdp_per_capita),gdp_per_capita > 0)|>
  mutate(gdp_group = case_when(gdp_per_capita < 5000 ~ "Low GDP",gdp_per_capita < 20000 ~ "Middle GDP",TRUE ~ "High GDP"),
         log_gdp = log(gdp_per_capita),
         gdp_group = factor(gdp_group,levels = c("Low GDP", "Middle GDP", "High GDP")))

sec4_n <- nrow(sec4_use)
sec4_countries <- n_distinct(sec4_use$iso3c)

stopifnot(sec4_n > 0)

# checking the correlation between poverty and life expectancy
sec4_correlation <- round(cor(sec4_use$poverty,sec4_use$life_expectancy),3)

# prepare the model1 and model2 for regression
sec4_model1 <- lm(life_expectancy ~ poverty + factor(year),data = sec4_use)
sec4_model2 <- lm(life_expectancy ~ poverty + log_gdp + factor(year),data = sec4_use)


```

#### 4.2 Data description

The analysis includes `r sec4_n` country-year observations from `r sec4_countries` countries with complete data. GDP per capita is categorised into three groups: low (below US$5,000), middle (US$5,000–19,999) and high (US$20,000 or above).

```{r Table-description}

sec4_summary <- sec4_use|>
  summarise(across(c(poverty, life_expectancy, gdp_per_capita),
                   list(Observations = ~n(),Mean = mean,Median = median,`Standard deviation`= sd,Min = min,Max = max),.names = "{.col}_{.fn}"))|>
  pivot_longer(everything(),names_to = c("Variable", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "^(poverty|life_expectancy|gdp_per_capita)_(.*)$")|>
  mutate(Variable = recode(Variable,poverty = "Poverty rate(%)",life_expectancy = "Life expectancy (years)",
                           gdp_per_capita = "GDP per capita (US$)"))

knitr::kable(sec4_summary,digits = 2,escape = FALSE,format = "html",
  caption = "<span style='color:black;font-size:14px;'>Table 1. Descriptive statistics of poverty and wellbeing</span>",
  align = c("l","r","r","r","r","r","r"))|>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = TRUE,font_size = 12,bootstrap_options = c("bordered","condensed"))

```

The above Table 1 provides descriptive statistics for 702 observations, showing substantial economic disparities across countries.The mean poverty rate (`r round(sec4_summary$Mean[1], 2)`%) is considerably higher than the median (`r round(sec4_summary$Median[1], 2)`%), indicating a right-skewed distribution where a few countries experience exceptionally high poverty. GDP per capita exhibits considerable variation (SD = US$24,606), highlighting significant differences in economic development.

#### 4.3 Data visualisation and analysis

Figure 1 illustrates a negative relationship between extreme poverty and life expectancy. Countries with higher poverty rates generally exhibit shorter life expectancy, although considerable variation exists. High GDP countries are concentrated at low poverty rates and typically have longer life expectancy, while low GDP countries tend to experience poorer health outcomes.However, variation within GDP groups suggests that other factors may also influence life expectancy.

  labs(title = NULL,x = "Poverty rate (%)",y = "Life expectancy (years)",color = "GDP group")+

```

Figure 2 compares the distribution of life expectancy across GDP groups. Median life expectancy increases from approximately 70 years in the low-GDP group to over 80 years in the high-GDP group. The low-GDP group also shows substantially greater variation, suggesting that countries with lower GDP per capita experience more diverse health outcomes.

Table 2 compares two regression models. Model 1 identifies a relationship between poverty and life expectancy, while Model 2 added log GDP per capita variable. 

```{r Table2-regression}

# Table 2 for regression comparison
sec4_regression <- data.frame(Variable = c("Poverty coefficient","Poverty p-value","GDP coefficient","GDP p-value","Adjusted R²"),
  `Model 1: Poverty only` = c(coef(sec4_model1)["poverty"],coef(summary(sec4_model1))["poverty", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    NA,NA,summary(sec4_model1)$adj.r.squared),
  `Model 2: Poverty + GDP` = c( coef(sec4_model2)["poverty"],coef(summary(sec4_model2))["poverty", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    coef(sec4_model2)["log_gdp"],coef(summary(sec4_model2))["log_gdp", "Pr(>|t|)"],summary(sec4_model2)$adj.r.squared),
  check.names = FALSE,row.names = NULL)

# Format numbers and p values
sec4_regression[,2:3] <- lapply(
  sec4_regression[,2:3],function(x) ifelse(is.na(x),"NA",sprintf("%.3f", x)))

# Display very small p-values as <0.001
p_rows <- sec4_regression$Variable %in% c("Poverty p-value", "GDP p-value")

sec4_regression[p_rows, 2:3] <- lapply(
  sec4_regression[p_rows, 2:3],function(x) {ifelse(x == "0.000","<0.001",x)})

kable(sec4_regression,row.names = FALSE,align = c("l", "r", "r"),format = "html",escape = FALSE,
      caption = "<span style='color:black;font-size:14px;'>Table 2. Comparison of regression models</span>")|>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = TRUE,font_size = 12,bootstrap_options = c("bordered","condensed"))

```

In Model 1, poverty is significantly negatively associated with life expectancy (β = −0.336, p < 0.001). After controlling for log GDP per capita in Model 2, the poverty coefficient decreases in magnitude to −0.131 but remains statistically significant (p < 0.001). Meanwhile, log GDP per capita shows a significant positive association with life expectancy (β = 3.402, p < 0.001). The increase in adjusted R² from 0.520 to 0.784 indicates that Model 2 fits the data better and explains more variation in life expectancy.

Overall, the findings suggest that higher extreme poverty is associated with lower life expectancy, even after accounting for GDP per capita. However, the weaker poverty coefficient in Model 2 suggests that economic development explains part of the observed relationship. The research by @yu2026 also highlights the complex relationship between poverty, economic development and population health. However, these findings only represent statistical associations and do no necessarily imply causation.

## Conclusion

This report examined the factors associated with poverty reduction across countries and identified disparities that persist despite economic development. The findings demonstrate that poverty is a multidimensional issue influenced by economic growth, income distribution and broader wellbeing.

The analysis of poverty trends revealed substantial global progress between 2002 and 2024, particularly in South Asia and East Asia and Pacific. However, regional improvements remain uneven, while considerable differences between international and national poverty rates highlight the importance of country-specific poverty definitions.

The analysis of income growth indicated that the bottom 40% generally kept pace with, and slightly exceeded, income growth for the whole population: the poorest grew faster in 64% of countries, with a median gap of 0.5 percentage points. Progress was uneven, however, and the bottom 40% fell behind in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, where only 22% of countries saw faster growth for the poorest. Bottom-40% incomes were also strongly associated with GDP per capita (correlation 0.94 on logged values), suggesting that economic development is important but does not guarantee equitable outcomes.

The wellbeing analysis demonstrated a significant negative association between extreme poverty and life expectancy. This relationship remained statistically significant after accounting for GDP per capita, indicating that poverty is associated with poorer health outcomes beyond differences in national income.

Several limitations should be acknowledged, including missing observations, inconsistent survey years, differences in national poverty definitions and the inability to establish causal relationships.

Overall, the findings highlight the importance of combining economic growth with inclusive development policies and improved access to essential services. Monitoring multiple poverty and wellbeing indicators is essential for identifying disadvantaged populations and supporting sustainable and equitable poverty reduction.
